content.body: Have you ever tried to split a set of items into two equal piles? Today we'll solve a classic puzzle: Partition Equal Subset Sum. We'll learn how to check if an array can be divided into two groups with equal totals using smart memory techniques.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
• Apply the 'remember what we've seen' mental model to subset problems
• Implement a dynamic programming approach using a Set to track achievable sums
• Explain why checking for previously seen sums prevents redundant calculations
content.title: What you'll learn
Try it
content.prompt: Can you split [1, 5, 11, 5] into two groups with equal sums?
content.successMessage: Good thinking! You might have tried combinations like 1+5+5=11 vs 11.

content.title: Try a bigger array
content.prompt: What about [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]? Can it be split equally?
content.successMessage: You're exploring combinations! The total is 28, so we need two groups summing to 14 each.

content.title: One more
content.prompt: Try [2, 2, 3, 5] - can it be partitioned equally?
content.successMessage: Nice exploration! You checked combinations like 2+3=5 vs 2+5=7 (not equal).

content.body: You just tried brute force - checking different combinations of numbers to see if they sum to half the total. For small arrays, this works, but it becomes overwhelming as arrays grow larger.
content.title: What you did

content.body: With 20 numbers, there are over a million possible combinations to check! We need a smarter approach that remembers what sums we can achieve as we go. Can't figure it out? Click Show me on the next step.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: Instead of re-checking combinations, we'll use a lookup structure (a Set) to remember all achievable sums so far. Each time we see a new number, we add it to existing sums to create new possibilities. This way, we build up knowledge incrementally without redundant work.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Think of it like a notebook where we write down every sum we can make. Before trying new combinations, we check our notebook to see if we've already achieved that sum.

content.body: We'll track achievable sums in a Set, starting with 0. For each number, we'll add it to every sum we've seen so far. If we ever reach exactly half the total, we've found our partition!
content.title: The approach

content.body:
1. Calculate total sum - if odd, return false immediately
2. Initialize a Set with 0 (we can always make sum 0)
3. For each number in the array:
   a. Create a new Set from current achievable sums
   b. For each sum in current Set, add the current number
   c. If we reach target sum, return true
4. If we finish without reaching target, return false
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Check if partition is possible
steps.instruction: First, let's handle the easy case. If the total sum is odd, we can't split it equally. Calculate the total sum and check if it's divisible by 2.
steps.hint: Use reduce to sum the array, then check if sum % 2 === 0
steps.expectedOutcome: The function should return false for odd sums, undefined for even sums (for now)
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've handled the base case correctly.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Remember to check if the remainder when dividing by 2 is not 0.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's think about this: if the total is odd, can we split it into two equal integer sums?

steps.title: Initialize our memory
steps.instruction: Now create a Set to track achievable sums. Start with 0 since we can always make sum 0 (by choosing no elements). Also calculate our target (half the total).
steps.hint: Create a new Set with 0 as the initial value
steps.expectedOutcome: A Set containing {0} and target calculated
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! Our notebook starts with 'we can make sum 0'.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. Remember to use 'new Set([0])' to initialize with 0.
steps.feedbackWrong: We need a Set data structure to remember sums. Start by saying we can make sum 0.

steps.title: Process each number
steps.instruction: Loop through each number in the array. For each number, we'll need to update our Set of achievable sums. Start by creating the loop structure.
steps.hint: Use for...of loop to iterate through nums
steps.expectedOutcome: A loop that iterates through all numbers
steps.feedbackCorrect: Good! Now we're ready to process each number.
steps.feedbackPartial: Check your loop syntax. You need to access each number in the array.
steps.feedbackWrong: We need to examine each number one by one. Use a for loop or for...of.

steps.title: Update achievable sums
steps.instruction: Inside the loop, create a new Set from current sums. For each existing sum, add the current number to create new achievable sums. This is where we 'remember what we've seen' and build new possibilities.
steps.hint: Use Array.from(sums) to iterate, then add (sum + num) to newSums
steps.expectedOutcome: newSums contains all previous sums plus (sum + num) for each sum
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! You're building up all possible sums incrementally.
steps.feedbackPartial: Remember to iterate through sums and add (sum + num) to newSums.
steps.feedbackWrong: For each sum we can already make, we can also make (sum + num) by including the current number.

steps.title: Check for target and update
steps.instruction: After creating new sums, check if we've reached our target. If so, return true immediately. Then update our main sums Set with the new possibilities.
steps.hint: Check if newSums.has(target), then update sums = newSums
steps.expectedOutcome: Early return if target found, otherwise update sums Set
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You're efficiently tracking progress and stopping early when possible.
steps.feedbackPartial: Don't forget to update the sums Set with newSums at the end of each iteration.
steps.feedbackWrong: We need to check if we've achieved our target sum, and update our memory for the next number.

steps.title: Final return
steps.instruction: If we finish the loop without finding the target, return false. The partition doesn't exist.
steps.hint: Add return false after the loop
steps.expectedOutcome: Complete function that returns true/false correctly
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! You've implemented the complete solution.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost done! What should we return if we never found the target?
steps.feedbackWrong: If we process all numbers and never reach the target, the partition doesn't exist.

content.body: Great work! You've learned how to solve Partition Equal Subset Sum using the 'remember what we've seen' approach. Key takeaways: 1) Use a Set to track achievable sums, 2) Build possibilities incrementally, 3) Check for the target early. This pattern applies to many subset problems where remembering previous results avoids exponential combinations.
